Mandrakes
MAN-drayks
noun
From the Greek mandragoras; a fragrant plant of the nightshade kind bearing yellow fruit, anciently reckoned a token of love and fruitfulness.

Biblical Definition

Mandrakes are the fruit of a low plant of the nightshade kind, sweet-smelling and golden, which ripened about the time of the wheat harvest and was anciently reputed among the nations to be a love-token and a help to fruitfulness. They come into the sacred story in the contention between Leah and Rachel, the wives of Jacob. “Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them unto his mother Leah” (Gen 30:14). Rachel, who was barren and envied her sister’s children, begged the mandrakes of Leah, and bought them with the price of Jacob’s company for a night; and so Leah conceived again (Gen 30:14–16). The passage shows the household of the patriarch entangled in rivalry, superstition, and the longing for children, and yet the LORD overruling all to build the house of Israel through the twelve sons He had purposed to give. It is God, not the mandrakes, who opens and shuts the womb; for it was Leah, who had the mandrakes and bartered them away, that conceived, while Rachel remained barren until God remembered her and Himself opened her womb (Gen 30:22). The mandrakes appear again among the delights of the garden in the Song of Solomon: “the mandrakes give a smell” (Son 7:13), a fragrant emblem of the fruitful love of the bridegroom and the bride. The plant thus stands at the meeting of human longing and divine providence, a reminder that the gift of children is from the LORD alone.

Webster 1828 Definition

A fragrant nightshade plant reputed a love-token; the fruit Reuben gathered, over which Leah and Rachel contended, though God alone opens the womb.

MANDRAKES, the fragrant fruit of a low nightshade plant.

Anciently reckoned a love-token and help to fruitfulness.

Reuben found them in the field in wheat harvest (Gen 30:14).

Leah and Rachel contended over them in their rivalry (Gen 30:15).

Their smell is named among the delights of the Song (Son 7:13).

Key Scripture

Gen 30:14 — "And Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them unto his mother Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, Give me, I pray thee, of thy son's mandrakes."

Gen 30:15 — "And she said unto her, Is it a small matter that thou hast taken my husband? and wouldest thou take away my son's mandrakes also? And Rachel said, Therefore he shall lie with thee to night for thy son's mandrakes."

Gen 30:16 — "And Jacob came out of the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him, and said, Thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee with my son's mandrakes. And he lay with her that night."

Son 7:13 — "The mandrakes give a smell, and at our gates are all manner of pleasant fruits, new and old, which I have laid up for thee, O my beloved."

Modern Corruption

An agrarian image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that the gift of children is from the LORD alone, not from charms or means.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD alone opens and shuts the womb, and that no plant or charm can supply what He withholds or accomplish what He has not purposed. The mandrakes were anciently reputed to aid fruitfulness, and Rachel coveted them in her barrenness; yet it was Leah, who bartered the mandrakes away, who conceived, while Rachel remained barren until God remembered her and Himself opened her womb. The narrative quietly rebukes the trust in means and tokens and exalts the providence of God over the building of His people.

The history also lays bare the rivalry and superstition that troubled even the household of the patriarch, and shows the LORD overruling such weakness to His own gracious ends. Out of the contention of Leah and Rachel God built the twelve tribes of Israel, fulfilling His covenant purpose through the tangled affections of men. The mandrakes that perfume the garden in the Song remind us that fruitfulness and conjugal love are good gifts of God, to be received from His hand and not sought by the devices of the heathen.

Hebrew Roots

From the Greek mandragoras, a fragrant nightshade plant reputed a love-token; the fruit Reuben gathered in wheat harvest.

Mandrakes — from Greek mandragoras.

A low nightshade plant with fragrant golden fruit.

Anciently reckoned a love-token and aid to fruitfulness.

Reuben found them in the field in wheat harvest (Gen 30:14).

Usage

"Like the mandrakes Rachel coveted, no charm or means can give what God alone bestows."

"The history teaches that the LORD opens and shuts the womb, building His people by His own purpose."

"The mandrakes of the Song remind us that fruitfulness and love are good gifts from the hand of God."
